title: Reel change; why he stayed south; the bank and Pullman porter work
summary: Charles refused offers to go north, left the bank in 1918 and worked as a Pullman porter until the armistice.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Here it's going now. This is Real Floor, Hippolyte Charles, April the 13th, 1963. You wanted to ask him about something? Mr. Charles, after the closing of Storyville in New Orleans, many of the musicians went up north. Would you tell us, for instance, why you stayed down south here most of the time as a musician?
I couldn't see going up north. The man was sent for me twice and I refused. Yeah, I couldn't see going nowhere but right there in New Orleans and I stayed there.
And you continued to work in the bank there?

I worked in the bank until 1918, when the First World War broke out, that's the time I left the bank, because they claimed the work wasn't essential. And I had to leave the bank and I went on a Pullman car. And right after the Amistad was signed I quit the Pullman car and went to play music and played music up until I quit.
Where'd you go on the Pullman car?
Pullman Porter. Where though? New Orleans, running from New Orleans all over.
Up and down the Mississippi Valley primarily?

No, we didn't. At first they had me on the SP. Then they took me off the SP, they had me on the LNN, running to Mobile. I was just running X-Tree. And when they put me on the regular line that was on the golf course, running to Alexandria. And that's why when I got to Mansoura, I rode almost to the one side. I said well that's the last. But I couldn't get along on the Pullman car.
